title: Building a Ride-Sharing App
subtitle: From scrappy prototype to nationwide service
description: Follow a ride-sharing app from a single-city experiment to a nationwide platform. You'll learn how real-time location tracking, race conditions, and microservice architectures shape the systems behind every ride you take.

stages.title: One City, Fifty Drivers

narrative.setup: You've launched a ride-sharing app in one city with fifty drivers. A rider opens the app, taps 'Request Ride,' and your server finds the nearest available driver. It's simple, it works, and the local press just wrote a nice article about you.

blocks.content:
Your ride-sharing app is live. A rider requests a ride, your [[node:server|server]] finds the nearest available driver and sends them the request. The driver accepts, picks up the rider, completes the trip.

Fifty drivers, a few hundred riders, one city. One [[node:server|server]], one [[node:database|database]].

blocks.label: Real-world analogy: the taxi dispatch office
blocks.content: Think of your system like a small-town taxi dispatch office. One person sits at a desk with a map and a list of drivers. A call comes in, they look at the map, radio the nearest driver, done. When you only have a handful of cars, one dispatcher can handle everything.

There's an important distinction in the data flowing through your system. Some is **persistent** -- trip history, payment records, user profiles. This goes in your [[glossary:database|database]].

Other data is **ephemeral** -- it changes constantly and you don't need it long-term. The key example: **driver locations**. Every few seconds, each [[node:driver|driver's phone]] sends a GPS update. These coordinates are only useful *right now*. Nobody cares where a driver stood 30 minutes ago when matching a new ride.

blocks.caption: A simple ride-sharing system -- one server does it all

blocks.content: **Ephemeral data** (driver locations, availability) and **persistent data** (trip records, payments) have fundamentally different storage needs. Using the wrong tool for the job will come back to bite you.

The matching logic is straightforward:

1. [[node:rider|Rider]] requests a ride with a pickup location
2. [[node:server|Server]] queries all available drivers and picks the closest
3. Driver has 15 seconds to accept
4. If they decline or time out, the server tries the next closest

With fifty drivers, this finishes in milliseconds.
At small scale, simple solutions are the *right* solutions. A straightforward loop that checks distances works perfectly for fifty drivers. The complexity will come on its own.

blocks.question: Your driver location data updates every 3 seconds per driver. With 50 drivers, that's roughly 17 GPS updates per second. Why might it be a bad idea to store every single one of these updates in your main database?

options.text: GPS data is too large for a database to handle
options.explanation: GPS coordinates are tiny -- just two decimal numbers. Size isn't the issue; it's the *frequency* of writes.

options.text: Writing to the database 17 times per second for data you'll throw away wastes resources and slows down queries that actually matter
options.explanation: Every database write takes effort -- disk I/O, transaction logging, index updates. Those writes compete with the reads and writes your app actually cares about, like recording trips or processing payments. Ephemeral data deserves an ephemeral store.
Databases handle GPS coordinates just fine -- many have specialized geospatial features. The issue is using the right tool for the job.

suggestedQuestions: What's the difference between ephemeral and persistent data?
How does GPS tracking actually work in a phone app?
Why not just keep everything in the database to keep things simple?

stages.title: Ten Cities, Five Thousand Drivers

narrative.setup: Your app is a hit. You've expanded to ten cities with five thousand drivers. Riders love the service. Investors are excited. You're hiring fast.
narrative.problem: Two problems hit at the same time. First, all those GPS updates -- now 1,700 per second across 5,000 drivers -- are hammering your database. Queries for trip history and payments are slowing to a crawl. Second, and more dangerously, you're getting reports of the same driver being assigned to two different riders simultaneously. Your matching system has a race condition.
narrative.resolution: You move ephemeral location data into Redis (a fast in-memory store), and add optimistic locking to your driver matching logic to prevent double-assignments.

blocks.content:
Two fires at the same time.

**Fire one: your [[node:database|database]] is drowning.** 5,000 drivers sending GPS updates every 3 seconds = ~1,700 writes per second of throwaway location data. The queries you actually care about (trips, payments, profiles) are getting slower.

**Fire two: ghost rides.** Riders are told a driver is coming, then get cancelled. Drivers receive requests while already en route to someone else.

The root cause of fire two: when two riders near the same driver request a ride simultaneously, the server checks availability for both, sees the driver is free, and assigns them to *both*. By the time the second assignment goes through, the driver is already taken.

blocks.label: Real-world analogy: the last item on the shelf
blocks.content: Two people in a store both spot the last item on the shelf at the same time. Both reach for it, both grab it, and both walk to checkout thinking they got it. That's a [[glossary:race-condition|race condition]] -- two processes acting on the same resource without knowing about each other.

## Fixing the database bottleneck

Move driver locations to [[node:redis|Redis]], an [[glossary:in-memory-store|in-memory store]]. Redis keeps everything in RAM and can handle hundreds of thousands of operations per second. Since driver locations are ephemeral -- you only care about the *latest* position -- old locations are simply overwritten.

blocks.caption: Redis handles ephemeral GPS data; the database handles persistent records

blocks.content: If Redis crashes, that data is gone. For driver locations, this is fine -- the next GPS ping repopulates in seconds. But never put data you can't afford to lose (like payment records) in an in-memory store alone.

## Fixing the race condition

The matching logic does: **Read** (is driver available?) → **Decide** (yes!) → **Write** (mark unavailable). Between steps 1 and 3, another request sneaks in.

The fix: [[glossary:consistency|optimistic locking]] -- making the check-and-write an **atomic operation** that can't be interrupted.

blocks.label: Real-world analogy: version numbers on a document
blocks.content: Optimistic locking works like a version number on a shared document. Before you save, you check: *"Is the version still the same as when I started editing?"* If yes, save and bump the version. If someone else changed it first, you know you need to retry. It's called "optimistic" because you assume there won't be a conflict and only check at the end.

In practice:

1. Read the driver's record, including a version number (e.g., version 5)
2. Decide to assign the driver
3. Write the assignment, but **only if the version is still 5**
4. If it is, success -- version becomes 6
5. If another request already changed it to 6, the write fails and your code retries with the next driver

Redis makes this even easier with built-in atomic commands -- "set this value only if it's currently X" in a single operation.

blocks.question: A new engineer suggests solving the race condition by locking the entire drivers table -- no one can read or write until the current matching is done. What's wrong with this?

options.text: It would work, but every ride request has to wait in line, even for drivers in completely different cities
options.explanation: This pessimistic lock prevents race conditions but creates a massive bottleneck. A ride being matched in New York blocks a request in Los Angeles for no reason. Optimistic locking is better because conflicts are rare -- you only pay the retry cost when two riders actually compete for the same driver.

options.text: Locking doesn't actually prevent race conditions
options.explanation: A full table lock would prevent race conditions -- the problem is it serializes every request, destroying performance at scale.

options.text: Redis doesn't support any kind of locking
options.explanation: Redis supports several locking mechanisms, including distributed locks. The issue is choosing the right *granularity* -- a table-wide lock is like closing an entire highway because of one pothole.

blocks.scenario: During a Friday night surge, 5% of ride matches fail on the first try due to version conflicts and need to retry. A team member suggests increasing the lock hold time to reduce conflicts.
blocks.question: Is increasing the lock hold time a good idea?

options.text: No -- longer lock times increase the window for conflicts and slow everything down
options.explanation: With optimistic locking, there's no lock being "held." A 5% retry rate during peak surge is actually healthy -- retries are fast (milliseconds) and the system self-corrects.

options.text: Yes -- holding the lock longer gives each match more time to complete cleanly
options.explanation: The longer any match takes, the more other requests pile up, and the more likely conflicts become. It's like solving a traffic jam by making every car drive slower.

options.text: Yes, but only during surge periods -- use a dynamic lock timer
options.explanation: Surge periods have the most concurrent requests, so longer lock times during surges would create the worst bottleneck exactly when you can least afford it.

blocks.label: Deep dive: how does Redis handle 100,000+ operations per second?
blocks.content:
Redis achieves its speed through a few key design choices:

**Everything is in memory.** RAM access is ~1,000x faster than disk.

**Single-threaded event loop.** Eliminates thread coordination overhead. Since each operation takes microseconds, one thread can process hundreds of thousands per second.

**Simple data structures.** Redis is a key-value store with lists, sets, and sorted sets -- no complex SQL queries.

For your app: `SET driver:1234:location "40.7128,-74.0060"` with a 30-second expiration. If a driver stops sending updates, their location automatically disappears.

suggestedQuestions: What happens if Redis crashes and all driver locations are lost?
How does optimistic locking compare to pessimistic locking?
Could you use Redis for everything instead of a traditional database?

stages.title: Nationwide at Scale

narrative.setup: Your app has gone nationwide. Fifty thousand drivers, millions of rides per month, and your engineering team has grown from 5 people to 50. The codebase is massive -- matching, payments, notifications, pricing, driver onboarding, and analytics all live in one giant application.
narrative.problem: At 2 AM on a Saturday, a bug in the payment processing code causes an unhandled exception. Because everything runs in a single application, the crash takes down the *entire system* -- including ride matching. For 12 agonizing minutes, no one in the country can request a ride. The next morning, your CEO's phone is ringing off the hook.
narrative.resolution: You break the monolith into microservices connected by a message queue, add monitoring and alerting, and implement circuit breakers so one failing service can't take down the rest.

blocks.content: A bug in your payment code -- nothing to do with ride matching -- took down your entire platform. This happened because your app is a [[glossary:microservices|monolith]]: one application where every feature shares the same process. When the payment code crashed the process, matching, notifications, and everything else went down with it.

blocks.label: Real-world analogy: the power strip
blocks.content: A monolith is like a power strip with every appliance in your house plugged into it -- refrigerator, TV, Wi-Fi router, lights. When someone trips over the cord, *everything* goes dark. What you need is separate circuits, so the kitchen keeps running even if the living room blows a fuse.

The solution: [[glossary:microservices|microservices]] -- independent services that each handle one part of the business:

- [[node:matching|Matching Service]] -- finds and assigns drivers
- [[node:payment|Payment Service]] -- handles charges, refunds, payouts
- [[node:notification|Notification Service]] -- push notifications and SMS
- **Pricing Service** -- fares and surge pricing
- **Trip Service** -- trip lifecycle and history

Each runs independently with its own database. If the [[node:payment|Payment Service]] crashes, riders can still get matched.

But how do services talk to each other? Direct calls create tight coupling -- if the [[node:notification|Notification Service]] is slow, the [[node:matching|Matching Service]] has to wait.

A better approach: a [[glossary:message-queue|message queue]]. The [[node:matching|Matching Service]] drops a message onto the [[node:queue|queue]]: *"Ride #4521 was matched, notify the rider."* The [[node:notification|Notification Service]] picks it up when ready.

blocks.label: Real-world analogy: the office to-do board
blocks.content: A message queue is like a to-do board in an office. Instead of tapping someone on the shoulder and standing there while they work, you write a task on a sticky note and put it on the board. They get to it when they can. Nobody is blocked, nothing is lost.

blocks.caption: Microservices communicate through a message queue -- no single failure takes down the system

blocks.content:
This is an [[glossary:event-driven|event-driven architecture]]. Services publish *events* ("ride requested," "driver matched," "trip completed") and other services subscribe to the ones they care about.

The Matching Service just says *"a match happened"* and moves on. Notification, Pricing, and Analytics all react independently.

Event-driven architecture shifts the question from *"what should I call next?"* to *"what just happened, and who cares?"* Adding new features becomes easy -- just subscribe a new service to existing events. No changes to running services.

## Making it resilient

What if the Payment Service is running but responding slowly? If the Trip Service waits for payment confirmation, slow payments back up everything.

A [[glossary:circuit-breaker|circuit breaker]] monitors calls to a service. If it detects too many errors or timeouts, it "trips" and stops sending requests, returning a fallback response instead. The Trip Service can complete the trip and queue payment for later -- rather than making the rider wait.

Microservices are not a free lunch. They introduce network calls (which can fail), distributed data management (which is complex), and operational overhead. Many teams adopt them too early. A well-structured monolith is often right until you genuinely have the scale and team size problems that microservices solve.

## Monitoring and failover

With five-plus services, you need [[glossary:monitoring|monitoring]] -- real-time visibility into every service's health:

- **Is it running?** (health checks)
- **Is it fast enough?** (latency metrics)
- **Is it correct?** (error rates)

When monitoring detects a problem, [[glossary:failover|failover]] kicks in. Each critical service runs on multiple instances. If one dies, traffic shifts to healthy instances automatically.

blocks.question: Your Notification Service goes down for 5 minutes. In a microservice architecture with a message queue, what happens to the ride notifications?

options.explanation: That would be true with direct synchronous calls. With a message queue, messages persist until consumed.

options.text: They pile up in the message queue and get processed once the Notification Service recovers
options.explanation: Messages are durable -- they persist in the queue until acknowledged. When the service recovers, it processes the backlog. Riders get notifications a few minutes late, but nothing is lost.

options.text: The Matching Service detects the failure and starts sending notifications itself
options.explanation: In a microservice architecture, services have clear responsibilities. The Matching Service shouldn't know how to send notifications. The message queue handles the gap.

blocks.scenario: New Year's Eve. Ride requests at 10x normal volume. Matching is keeping up, but the Payment Service is buckling -- response times went from 200ms to 8 seconds. Riders stare at 'Processing payment...' and some force-quit and retry, making it worse.
blocks.question: What's the best immediate response?

options.text: Trip the circuit breaker on payments -- complete trips immediately, queue payments for later
options.explanation: The ride is the core value -- the rider got from A to B. Payment can be processed asynchronously. Tripping the circuit breaker clears the spinning screens, stops the force-quit cascade, and payments settle minutes later.

options.text: Add more instances of the Payment Service to handle the load
options.explanation: Right long-term move, but spinning up new instances takes time. Riders are staring at frozen screens *now*. You need an immediate fix, then scale up to prevent it next time.

options.text: Throttle incoming ride requests to reduce overall system load
options.explanation: Refusing riders on the busiest night of the year is terrible for business. Only the Payment Service is struggling -- a targeted fix (circuit breaker) addresses the bottleneck without turning anyone away.

blocks.label: Deep dive: what does eventual consistency look like in microservices?
blocks.content:
With one database, everything was consistent by default. With microservices, each service has its own database and they communicate through events.

This means brief moments where services disagree. For example:

1. Matching Service assigns a driver and publishes "ride matched"
2. For a few hundred milliseconds, the Trip Service hasn't processed that event
3. Querying the Trip Service during that gap returns no match

This is [[glossary:eventual-consistency|eventual consistency]] -- the system will *eventually* agree, but there's a brief window of disagreement.

Rule of thumb: if split-second accuracy matters (deducting money), use synchronous calls. If a few hundred milliseconds of delay is acceptable (analytics dashboards), use events.

**Synchronous when the caller needs the answer to continue, asynchronous when it just needs to announce what happened.** Matching needs to confirm a payment hold before dispatching (synchronous). It doesn't need to wait for the analytics dashboard (asynchronous).
